kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-06.title: Right triangle
kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-06.body:
Let the hexagon have side 1. The vertical side of the triangle joins two vertices that are one vertex apart, so it is a short diagonal of length $\sqrt3$, and it is perpendicular to the top side of the hexagon (the hexagon is symmetric about the horizontal line through its centre, so this diagonal is vertical while the top side is horizontal).

So the triangle has a right angle at the top-left vertex, with legs 1 (top side) and $\sqrt3$ (short diagonal). The angle $x$ lies opposite the leg of length 1, so $\tan x = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ and $x = 30°$.

**Answer: (B) 30**

kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-06.title: Angles in the hexagon
kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-06.body:
The third side of the triangle is a long diagonal through the centre; it bisects the 120° angle at the bottom-left vertex, making 60° with the bottom side. The vertical side of the triangle is perpendicular to the bottom side (90°). Hence $x = 90° - 60° = 30°$.

**Answer: (B) 30**

kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-11.title: Laps per hour
kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-11.body:
The bear needs 30 minutes per lap and the walrus 24 minutes. In 120 minutes (the least common multiple of 24 and 30) the walrus swims 5 laps and the bear 4 laps, so the walrus is exactly one lap ahead. Before that the gap is less than one lap, since it grows steadily.

**Answer: (C) 120**

kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-11.title: Equation
kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-11.body:
After $t$ minutes the walrus has swum $\frac{t}{24}$ laps and the bear $\frac{t}{30}$ laps. We need $\frac{t}{24} - \frac{t}{30} = 1$, i.e. $\frac{t}{120} = 1$, so $t = 120$.

**Answer: (C) 120**

kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-13.title: Turn averages into sums
kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-13.body:
The three ages add up to 3 × 10 = 30. The two pairs add up to 22 and 24. The sister missing from the first pair is 30 − 22 = 8, and the one missing from the second pair is 30 − 24 = 6. The third sister is 30 − 8 − 6 = 16.

Check: 8 + 16 = 24 (average 12) and 6 + 16 = 22 (average 11). ✓

**Answer: (E) 16**

kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-16.title: Chase the angles
kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-16.body:
Let $\angle BAC = a$.

- $AD = DB$: $\angle ABD = a$, so the exterior angle $\angle BDC = 2a$.
- $CE = CD$ (and $E$ lies on $BD$): $\angle CED = \angle CDE = 2a$.
- $BE = EC$: $\angle EBC = \angle ECB$, and the exterior angle $\angle CED = \angle EBC + \angle ECB$, so $\angle EBC = a$.

Then $\angle ABC = \angle ABD + \angle DBC = a + a = 2a$, and $\angle ACB = \angle ABC = 2a$. The angle sum gives $a + 2a + 2a = 180°$, so $a = 36°$.

**Answer: (E) 36**

kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-16.title: Check the answer
kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-16.body:
With $\angle A = 36°$: $\angle B = \angle C = 72°$; $\angle ABD = 36°$, $\angle DBC = 36°$, $\angle BDC = 72°$, $\angle CED = 72°$, $\angle DCE = 36°$, $\angle ECB = 36°$. All three small triangles are isosceles as required.

**Answer: (E) 36**

kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-21.title: Three hexagons
kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-21.body:
The shape consists of three hexagons, each made of 6 small triangles, and every pair of hexagons shares one edge; the three shared edges meet at the centre point. Every tile covers two neighbouring triangles.

**Case 1: no tile crosses a shared edge.** Then each hexagon is tiled on its own. The 6 triangles of a hexagon form a ring, and a ring of 6 can be split into neighbouring pairs in exactly 2 ways. That gives $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$ tilings.

**Case 2: some tile crosses a shared edge.** Each hexagon has 6 triangles; a tile crossing out of it uses one of them, so an even number of crossing tiles must touch each hexagon (otherwise an odd number of triangles is left inside it). Each hexagon touches only two shared edges, so either both or none of its shared edges are crossed. If one shared edge is crossed, both its hexagons need their other shared edge crossed as well, so all three shared edges are crossed. Then each hexagon loses its two triangles at the centre, leaving a strip of 4 triangles, which can be tiled in exactly 1 way. That gives 1 tiling.

Total: $8 + 1 = 9$.

**Answer: (D) 9**

kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-27.title: Gain per removed cube
kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-27.body:
The big cube has surface $6 \cdot 16 = 96$. We need $1.5 \cdot 96 = 144$, i.e. a gain of 48.

When we take out a small cube that has $k$ faces on the outside, those $k$ faces disappear and its other $6-k$ faces become new surface: the change is $6 - 2k$. A cube we can take out has at least one outside face, so each removal gains at most $6 - 2 = 4$. Hence at least $48 \div 4 = 12$ cubes are needed.

Twelve is enough: take out 2 of the 4 centre cubes on each of the 6 faces, choosing two that do not touch (diagonally opposite). Each such cube has exactly 1 outside face and all its other neighbours stay in place, so each gains 4: total $12 \cdot 4 = 48$.

**Answer: (D) 12**

kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-29.title: Use the 30-60-90 triangle
kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-29.body:
The fold sends $A$ to $C$, so $EA = EC$. Triangle $EBC$ has a right angle at $B$ and $\angle ECB = 30°$, so the side opposite the 30° angle is half the hypotenuse: $EB = \frac12 EC = \frac12 EA$.

So $AB = AE + EB = 3\,EB$, and
$$[ABCD] = AB \cdot BC = 3\,EB\cdot BC = 6 \cdot \tfrac12 EB\cdot BC = 6 \cdot 15 = 90.$$

**Answer: (A) 90 cm²**

kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-29.title: Compare triangles
kangaroo-ca-2022-g0708-29.body:
Triangle $AEC$ has base $AE = 2\,EB$ and the same height $BC$ as triangle $EBC$, so its area is 30. Triangle $ABC$ = $AEC$ + $EBC$ = 45, which is half the rectangle. Rectangle: 90 cm².

**Answer: (A) 90 cm²**
